newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus to weigh on dollar.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus to weigh on dollar.

text.p: Japan's ballooning trade surplus is likely to continuing weighing on the dollar over the medium term, currency traders in Tokyo said on Wednesday.
The dollar's downside, however, may be limited in the short-run as trade problems are unlikely to be a major issue at the Group of Seven industrialised nations' summit in Denver on June 20-22.
Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus surged to 738.27 billion yen ($6.53 billion) in May, more than trebling from a year earlier, the Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday.

"After recent surges in Japan's trade surplus, Japanese exporters will probably lower their dollar-selling target levels. This should make the dollar's upside heavy," said a manager at a major Japanese city bank who declined to be named.
Last week, exporter offers were seen above 115 yen. After the release of May trade data, some of them have lowered their offers to around 113.50 yen, traders said.
Opinions were divided how far the dollar might fall versus the Japanese currency in the medium term.

The dollar's fall below 110 yen cannot be ruled out, but seems unlikely, said Makoto Miyazaki, chief manager of foreign exchange group in the foreign exchange and treasury division at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.

"If the U.S. economy slows down, Japan's export growth may not maintain the current strength. Moreover, Japanese automakers' new production facilities in North American and Asia will be completed next year. Hence, there is a view that Japan's trade surplus may be already at the peak," Miyazaki said.
Japanese financial authorities are likely to intervene if the dollar falls below 110 yen, traders said.

"If the dollar dips below 110 yen, exporters may be forced to revise down their profit outlook. A break of that level could also prompt speculators to target 105 yen or even 100 yen. So authorities should want to avoid it," Miyazaki said.
The city bank manager who declined to be identified said 110 yen may not prove to be the medium-term bottom.

"Japan does not want a 'weak' yen. That's the reason why the authorities have knocked the dollar below 120 yen. What is very clear is that 120 yen is the ceiling the Japanese authorities are willing to tolerate. The floor, however, is not yet clear. It may not necessarily be 110 yen," he said.
Traders agreed that the dollar's downside is limited in the near term as Japan's trade surplus is unlikely to be a major subject at the upcoming G7 summit meeting.
Position-squaring might even provide a short-term support to the greenback after the summit, they said.

"Worries about Japan's trade surplus being highlighted at the Denver summit have waned after senior MOF official Sakakibara denied that possibility last week," said Ichiro Ikeda, director and head of sales of the foreign exchange department at Credit Suisse First Boston in Tokyo.

Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, was quoted by a participant in a closed seminar last Thursday as saying that Japan's trade surplus was unlikely to be a major issue at the Denver summit.

"To counter the growing trade surplus, Japanese authorities have let the dollar fall sharply from above 127 yen in May. The U.S. authorities are aware that it would take time for forex adjustments to have an effect on trade balance," Ikeda said.

U.S. Treasury Robert Rubin said last Thursday that a sustained rise in Japan's trade surplus could hurt global growth but one could not judge whether the surplus was rising on a sustained basis by looking at "a month or quarter." ($1=113 yen)
